plan.title: Plate Tectonics: A Moving Planet
plan.hook: Connect slow plate motion to new crust, mountain building and sudden earthquakes.
objectives: Describe what a tectonic plate contains.
Distinguish earthquake magnitude, intensity and prediction.

sections.heading: The moving pieces include more than crust
sections.body:
A tectonic plate is a piece of lithosphere: crust plus rigid uppermost mantle. It can carry oceanic crust, continental crust, or both. A coastline is therefore not necessarily a plate boundary.

Below the lithosphere, hotter mantle material can deform and flow over long timescales while remaining mostly solid. Plates do not float on a global ocean of liquid magma. Timescale matters: a material can respond rigidly to a quick disturbance yet deform under sustained stress.

Plate motion reflects gravity and internal heat, including effects associated with sinking dense slabs, elevated ocean ridges and mantle flow. One cartoon conveyor belt cannot describe every detail.

At a hypothetical steady 3 cm/year, movement over 10 million years is 30 million centimetres, or 300 km. Small annual motion becomes enormous geological displacement. The constant rate and direction are simplifying assumptions, not a claim about every plate through time.
sections.visual: The rigid lithosphere contains crust and the uppermost mantle. It moves over hotter mantle rock that deforms slowly while remaining mostly solid. Plate speed is slow on a human timescale, but substantial over millions of years.

questions.q: Why is “continents floating on liquid magma” misleading?
questions.hint: Correct both the moving object and the material below it.
questions.answer: Lithospheric plates move, and the underlying mantle is mostly solid but slowly deformable. Plate outlines do not simply follow continents.

sections.heading: Pull apart, push together, slide past
sections.body:
At a divergent boundary, plates move apart. At mid-ocean ridges, rising mantle can partially melt as pressure decreases, and magma cools to create new oceanic crust. The gap does not expose Earth's core.

At a convergent boundary, plates approach. Dense oceanic lithosphere can descend at a subduction zone. Water released from the descending slab helps promote melting in the overlying mantle, feeding many volcanic arcs. Continental collision instead can produce extensive shortening and crustal thickening that build mountain ranges.

At a transform boundary, motion is mainly sideways. This idealised boundary motion does not systematically create or destroy crust, but faults can produce powerful earthquakes. A lack of volcanoes does not establish safety.

Real boundary zones can be broad and complicated. Earthquake depths, volcanic patterns, topography and measured surface motion provide complementary evidence; a single landscape photograph rarely establishes the entire mechanism.
sections.visual: Divergent plates move apart, transform plates slide past one another, and convergent plates move together. This convergent example shows one plate descending beneath another; other collisions can build mountain belts.

questions.q: Does the absence of a volcanic chain prove a plate boundary is inactive?
questions.answer: No. A transform fault can accumulate stress and generate earthquakes without a volcanic arc.

sections.heading: Slow loading can release suddenly
sections.body:
Friction can lock a fault while nearby rock slowly deforms under tectonic stress. When part of the fault slips, stored elastic energy is released as seismic waves. Long loading followed by abrupt slip explains how slow plate motion can produce sudden shaking.

The focus, or hypocentre, is where rupture starts underground. The epicentre is the surface point directly above it. Rupture can spread across a large fault area, so the earthquake is not confined to one mathematical point.

Magnitude describes the earthquake's source size. Intensity describes shaking effects at a particular location. One earthquake can produce different intensities because distance, depth and ground conditions differ; building vulnerability also affects damage.

Scientists estimate hazards and probabilities, but cannot reliably predict the exact time, location and magnitude of a future earthquake. Preparedness remains useful despite that limit. A quiet period is neither proof of safety nor an exact countdown to a large event.
sections.visual: A locked fault can accumulate elastic strain as plates continue moving. Sudden slip releases some of that stored energy as seismic waves. The rings show the idea of outward propagation, not a prediction of rupture timing.

questions.q: Why can one earthquake cause different damage at two nearby places?
questions.hint: Separate source size, local shaking and building vulnerability.
questions.answer: Ground conditions and wave paths change shaking, while buildings differ in vulnerability. Equal distance does not guarantee equal effects.

questions.q: What does a lithospheric plate contain?
questions.explain: The lithosphere includes crust and uppermost rigid mantle; a plate can contain continental and oceanic regions.

questions.q: At a steady 3 cm/year, how far does a plate move in 10 million years?
questions.explain: The product is 30,000,000 cm. Dividing by 100,000 cm/km gives 300 km.
Transform boundaries accommodate mainly lateral motion. Earthquakes can occur without ridge-like crust production.

questions.q: Which process forms new oceanic crust?
choices: Magma cooling near a spreading mid-ocean ridge
questions.explain: Partial melting beneath ridges supplies magma that can cool into new oceanic crust. Sediment deposition is different.

choices: The surface point directly above the rupture’s start
questions.explain: The underground starting location is the focus. The epicentre lies above it at the surface.

questions.q: Which statement best reflects earthquake forecasting limits?
choices: Hazard probabilities are useful, but exact future time, place and magnitude cannot be reliably predicted
Every fault repeats on an exact calendar
A quiet month guarantees a safe year
questions.explain: Useful hazard estimates do not require precise event prediction. Fault behaviour and local shaking remain variable.
